chunks: Humayd ibn Ziyad from Ibn Sama'ah from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamzah from Ali ibn Yaqteen from Al-Abd Al-Salih (peace be upon him) said:
I asked him about a man who married his slave to a free girl, so he said: The divorce is in the hand of the slave.
He said, And I asked him about a man who married his slave girl to a free man, so he said: The divorce is in the hand of the free man.
And I asked him about a man who married his slave to his slave girl, so he said: The divorce is in the hand of the master.
And I asked him about a man who bought a slave girl and for her was a slave husband, so he said: Selling her is her divorce.
ai.seo_question: Who has the right to divorce when a master marries his slave to a free person or another slave?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi clarifies the juridical nuances of 'talaq bi'd-y al-sayyid' (divorce by the master's hand) versus the slave's autonomous right, distinguishing between the status of the spouses and the master's ownership. It reflects the Shia scholarly understanding that while the master controls the marital bond of his slaves, the specific configuration determines who exercises the final authority to dissolve it, including the unique case where selling a married slave woman automatically terminates the marriage. These rulings underscore the interplay between property rights and personal status in classical Islamic family law.
